captive_summary: This is a direction-test case, not a captive finding. The Andes Energy Terminal (AET), a proposed LNG import project near Buenaventura, Valle del Cauca, is itself designed as a 5-part integrated development: LNG reception terminal, land-based regasification plant, LNG truck-loading terminal, a power plant, and gas/electrical transmission infrastructure. The project's own chairman describes the power plant as serving 'southwest and central Colombia's energy needs' — i.e. the co-located Andes Energy power station (GOGPT: 400 MW, 2 units, 0.48 km away) is a merchant plant the terminal is built to FEED, the opposite of captive power. No source describes a separate captive plant powering the regas terminal's own operations.
confirmed_how: Black & Veatch completed a feasibility study for AET (site assessment, design/financial estimates, climate resilience/financing); reported via Offshore-Energy.biz, which quotes AET Chairman Manuel Tenorio on the Pacific-coast gas deficit driving the project, and Black & Veatch's Laszlo von Lazar on 'the project's capacity to serve southwest and central Colombia's energy needs.' The article states directly: 'The AET project comprises an LNG terminal for receiving imported LNG, a land-based regasification plant, an LNG truck loading terminal, a power plant, and associated gas and electrical transmission infrastructure.'

verification_log.note: confirms AET's own 5-component design including 'a power plant' serving the regional grid

gogpt_prior_assessment: The single GOGPT neighbor, Andes Energy power station (400 MW, 2 units, 0.48 km, gogpt_captive=false, shelved), IS the power plant named in AET's own project description above — this is the PowerPlantsSupplied relationship (gas OUT to a merchant plant), not a captive plant powering the terminal. GEM's shard already records this as power_plants_supplied='Andes Energy power station', consistent with this finding.
gogpt_candidate_basis: GOGPT record already exists (Andes Energy power station); and in any case the relationship is PowerPlantsSupplied, not captive, so it would never be added on captive-power grounds.
status_or_other_findings: Both AET and its power-station component are listed as shelved/not advancing per GOGPT status metadata seen in the neighbor file; not independently verified here, flagging only.
notes: Textbook direction-test case per SOP: terminal built expressly to fuel an adjacent merchant power plant, not to power itself. No captive plant for the regas terminal's own load was found or expected here — do not confuse the Andes Energy power station's existence with a captive finding.

hardware_summary: Wärtsilä-Hyundai dual-fuel diesel-electric (DFDE) generator sets aboard the FSRU Höegh Grace (Hyundai Heavy Industries-built, 170,000 cbm, Mark III membrane containment) — the vessel's own power source while providing FSRU services to SPEC at Cartagena; no separate shore-side captive plant.
fuel_basis: DFDE = Dual-Fuel Diesel-Electric: the vessel's generator engines can burn gas fuel (typically boil-off gas) as well as diesel to produce the electric power that runs the ship's own systems and, when underway, its propulsion motors. Established via Höegh LNG's own naming release for Höegh Grace (built at Hyundai Heavy Industries) describing 'a Wärtsila-Hyundai DFDE engine', corroborated by an independent trade outlet's description of sister FSRU Höegh Gannet (same fleet, same builder, same 170,000 cbm class) as having 'dual-fuel diesel-electric (DFDE) propulsion'.
captive_summary: The FSRU Höegh Grace, which has provided SPEC's Cartagena import service since 2016, is built with Wärtsilä-Hyundai DFDE (dual-fuel diesel-electric) generating engines — this is the vessel's own onboard power generation under the FSRU-onboard convention, and it is a YES regardless of the fact no specific generating MW figure is publicly disclosed for this hull. No electric_mw figure was found in either source, so it is left blank per the rule that an undisclosed MW does not block a YES once on-site generation is documented.
confirmed_how: Offshore-Energy.biz (World Maritime News), 'Höegh LNG Names 6th FSRU at HHI' (Apr 15, 2015): 'The 249-long FSRU boasts a Mark III membrane containment system and a Wärtsila-Hyundai DFDE engine' — naming the vessel that became Höegh Grace, delivered Q2 2015/2016 and sent to Cartagena for SPEC. Corroborated by Marine Insight's article on sister-ship Höegh Gannet (delivered 2018, same 170,000 cbm HHI-built class): 'dual-fuel diesel-electric (DFDE) propulsion.' Höegh Evi's own current fleet page (hoeghevi.com/about/fleet) independently confirms Höegh Grace is an FSRU built 2016, serving customer 'SPEC – Sociedad Portuaria El Cayao' at Cartagena, Colombia — confirming vessel identity/deployment (not itself cited for the power claim).

verification_log.note: primary naming release for the vessel that became Höegh Grace, states 'Wärtsila-Hyundai DFDE engine'
independent publisher corroborating DFDE propulsion/generation across the same Höegh/HHI FSRU class
